title: SDSU guard Nick Anderson had knee surgery in June, but there's a chance he may play this season
text:
The New Aztec, who averaged 15.5 points for Rice last season while shooting 40% from 3-point range, is already two to three weeks ahead of a typical ACL rehab timeline.
Rice guard Nick Anderson, right, drives as he is defended by Tennessee guard Ethan Burg, left, during the second half of an NCAA college basketball game Monday, Nov. 17, 2025, in Knoxville, Tenn.
A few weeks ago, during a break in practice, Nick Anderson wandered over to a basket, jumped, spun in mid-air and dunked. It speaks to the accelerated nature of Anderson’s recovery from knee surgery in early June to repair a torn anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that typically takes nine to 12 months to fully heal. After two months, Anderson was already dunking.in May, the math said he would miss the entire 2026-27 season.
And Anderson still might, but the chances of seeing him in uniform, perhaps by January, remain a tantalizing possibility for the 6-foot-3 guard“I’ve always recovered from everything pretty quickly,” Anderson said.
“I know it’s a ligament, but honestly I thought I’d bounce back a lot quicker than people expected. ” He’s already two to three weeks ahead of a typical ACL rehab timeline, running on an anti-gravity treadmill, doing some lateral movement, shooting in stationary drills. At his current pace, he estimates he could be a full practice participant by late December — less than seven months after surgery.
He applied for a medical waiver with the NCAA in July and expects to hear back sometime during the fall. The tricky part is he already received one medical waiver — for a foot injury at Prairie View A&M during his third college season — and now is requesting another for what would be a sixth year of college eligibility. The NCAA recently passed five-for-five legislation, granting athletes five years to play five seasons.
But athletes who started their college careers earlier are grandfathered into the old regulations, which, in some cases, granted multiple medical waivers that extended college stays past five years. The plan: If he gets another medical waiver, he’ll sit out this season and play for the Aztecs in 2027-28.
“I feel very hopeful about it,” Anderson said of the waiver, “but there’s a lot going on with the NCAA right now. I’m just trying to prepare myself for both scenarios. I don’t want to be let down if I was really thinking a waiver would be .
“It’s been an interesting battle, trying to stay motivated every day when you don’t necessarily know what you’re working toward. ” So he arrives at the practice facility each morning at 8:30 for a rehab session with Ibarra, followed by weightlifting with strength coach Daniel Marshall, followed by shooting, followed by observing practice , followed by more treatment. Soon, he may add another shooting workout.
He’ll continue on an accelerated pace until the NCAA rules on his waiver. If he gets it, he can take a more patient approach. If not, full-steam ahead.
“Sergio and the doctors are in charge of the rehab with him,” coach Brian Dutcher said, “so it’s not something where I’m saying, ‘Boy, we’re going to have him available in January. ’ There are a lot of things involved before we get to the point where we consider playing him.
“If he’s available in January, then we’ll have a choice to make based on what the appeal is doing. If it’s in his best interest to play and the team’s best interest, then we’ll find a way to do that. ”, a 6-7 wing from France who spent the last two seasons at Oregon State. He’s been arguably the biggest surprise of summer and fall workouts, consistently knocking down 3-pointers while adding length and athleticism on the defensive end.
“Isaiah is a good player,” Dutcher said. “If Nick doesn’t tear his ACL, we probably aren’t looking for Isaiah. That worked out for Isaiah and for us. ”
